# Residential Tour Leader Handbook

Fictional Cedar Lantern Dance Studio. Training fixture only; no real studio policy.

## A studio residential trip
The residential tour is a supervised trip with overnight accommodation and group activities. It is separate from the daily campus shuttle and from a family arranging its own holiday around a performance. Every participant has a named travel group and a named overnight lead. The tour register records departure, arrival, planned handovers and the emergency contact route. Public itineraries contain meeting points but omit private room assignments.

A signed residential-tour consent form must reach the tour leader 28 calendar days before departure. The form covers the named trip and does not carry over to the next year. Families tell the leader about an amended emergency contact rather than crossing out the only copy on travel day. A place is not confirmed by bringing a packed suitcase to the departure point without the recorded consent.

Each residential-tour participant may bring one main bag weighing at most 12 kilograms plus one small day bag. Instruments assigned for the group performance are handled on the equipment inventory and do not count as personal day bags. Families label luggage with the participant's name and group colour; no home address is needed on the outside. A participant must be able to identify their own bag at a group collection.

## Medication and individual support
All scheduled tour medication must be handed to the designated medicines lead in its original labelled packaging at departure. The medicines lead checks the written schedule privately. The leader does not copy a student's medical details into a public room chart. The night-support notes describe a narrow exception for a recorded self-carried rescue inhaler; ordinary scheduled medication still follows the handover rule.

A family discusses support arrangements before the trip rather than assuming that a familiar classroom practice transfers automatically to a residential setting. The leader records agreed arrangements and shares only what each responsible adult needs to know. A buddy can help find a meeting point, but is not made responsible for another child's medication or personal care.

## Lights-out instruction and unresolved difference
The tour leader handbook sets residential-trip lights-out at 21:30. The current night-support notes state another time for the same residential trip. Both instructions apply to the same cohort and dates, and no published authority order resolves them. Staff should bring both instructions to the trip lead before giving a definitive time. The 21:30 coach return planned for a different excursion must not be substituted as evidence for lights-out.

## Rooms, keys and handovers
Participants may enter only their assigned sleeping room unless a staff lead explicitly accompanies a room visit. A friend sending a message is not staff permission. Room keys remain with the assigned staff lead during group activities. Staff do not disclose one student's room number to a visitor without checking the handover arrangement. A forgotten jumper can be fetched through the desk rather than by asking another participant to search a room alone.

The leader carries a room allocation copy in a closed folder. If a room becomes unusable, the leader records the reassignment, updates the emergency roll and informs the relevant family privately. A handwritten change on a corridor notice is insufficient. Keep the old allocation as an audit note so that staff know which version they previously saw.

## Delays and return travel
A delay message states the revised meeting place and the next planned update. It should not promise that traffic will clear at a particular minute. The leader checks the actual travel situation and then gives families a confirmed handover window. A parent collecting early signs the handover record; an informal wave across a car park does not complete responsibility transfer.

## Planning example
For the Lakeside residential visit, the leader gathers the named consent forms before confirming final room numbers. At departure the medicines lead checks scheduled medicine and its packaging. A participant's separate rescue-inhaler plan is checked against the night-support exception rather than treated as a blanket permission for all medication. During the visit an agreed room reassignment is entered in both the allocation and emergency roll. Before the evening briefing, staff reconcile the conflicting lights-out instructions through the trip lead instead of selecting whichever time is easier for that night's timetable.

## Visitor and family boundaries
A family attending the same public performance may meet their child only through the recorded handover arrangement. Buying a ticket or staying in a nearby hotel does not give access to the group's sleeping corridor. The leader explains the meeting place and who will sign responsibility over. If a parent changes plans, the leader checks the new arrangement before moving the participant off the group roll. The staff list should remain usable in an emergency and must not depend on a teacher remembering an informal conversation.

## Group equipment and meals
Shared costumes and portable speakers travel on the tour equipment inventory. Staff check them separately from personal luggage so that a missing prop does not lead to a search through a student's private bag without a clear reason. The leader records agreed meal arrangements through the private planning route. The handbook does not promise that a venue kitchen can meet every request made after arrival. Where a planned meal changes, the leader checks the individual's arrangement and gives a factual update rather than assuming all students can swap dishes.
